title: Consumer groups and rebalancing
goal: By the end you can explain how a consumer group divides partitions among its members, hand a partition's bookmark over cleanly when it moves, say what eager, cooperative and the new KIP-848 protocol each stop during a rebalance, and pick the settings that decide when a member is thrown out.

warmup.q: A group of three consumers reads a 6-partition topic with Kafka 4.4's default consumer settings. A fourth consumer starts. While the group rebalances, how many of the six partitions stop being processed?
options: Only the one or two partitions that move to the new consumer
All six: by default every member hands back every partition before the new assignment arrives
None: rebalancing happens in a background thread
Only the partitions of the busiest consumer
warmup.why: The client defaults to the classic protocol, and the default `partition.assignment.strategy` list, `[RangeAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor]`, uses Range, an eager assignor. Under eager rebalancing every member revokes all of its partitions before it rejoins, so the whole group stops. The first option describes what cooperative rebalancing and the new protocol (`group.protocol=consumer`) do. You have to choose them.

sections.h: A group divides the partitions, one owner each
sections.body:
One ledger consumer applies about 8 payments a second: each one waits 120 ms for the card issuer. At the end of the month the `payments` topic receives 30 a second. A single consumer falls 22 payments further behind every second, which is 79,200 after an hour. You need four of them.

The simplest idea is to start four copies of the service. If each copy reads the whole topic, as lesson 1 of this track showed every reader can, then every payment is applied four times. The next idea is to share the records the way a queue would: whoever is free takes the next one. That breaks two things you rely on. Lesson 4 put all of acct-7's records in one partition, in order, so its capture never overtakes its authorization; with two consumers on one partition, the capture can be applied first. And lesson 6's bookmark is one number per partition, which only works if one reader moves it.

Kafka shares the work by partition instead. A **consumer group** is a set of consumers with the same `group.id`. The group gives each partition to exactly one member, and a member can own several. With six partitions and three members, each member owns two. Inside a partition, one reader keeps the order. And each partition still has one committed offset for the group. A second group, such as `fraud-check`, divides the same partitions in its own way, with its own bookmarks (figure).

Two consequences follow. Parallelism stops at the partition count: a seventh member of a group on six partitions gets nothing and sits idle. And moving work around means moving partitions, which the rest of this lesson is about.

Who decides who owns what? One broker is the group's **coordinator**: the broker that leads the partition of `__consumer_offsets` where the group's commits live. Members tell it they are alive. An **assignor** turns "these members, these partitions" into a map from partition to member, the assignment. There are three classic recipes. Range hands each member a block of consecutive partitions, topic by topic. Round robin deals all partitions out like cards. Sticky balances the group and moves as few partitions as possible. They differ more than you might expect: with two topics of three partitions and two members, range gives one member four partitions and the other two, and round robin gives both three. The lab builds all three.

To join a group, set `group.id` and call `subscribe` instead of `assign`:

```java
var config = Map.<String, Object>of(
        "bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092",
        "group.id", "ledger",                 // the group: members share its partitions
        "group.protocol", "consumer",         // the new rebalance protocol (section 3)
        "enable.auto.commit", false,
        "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class,
        "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class);
var consumer = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(config);
consumer.subscribe(List.of("payments"));      // the group decides which partitions this member reads
```

```kotlin
val config = mapOf<String, Any>(
    "bootstrap.servers" to "localhost:9092",
    "group.id" to "ledger",                   // the group: members share its partitions
    "group.protocol" to "consumer",           // the new rebalance protocol (section 3)
    "enable.auto.commit" to false,
    "key.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java,
    "value.deserializer" to StringDeserializer::class.java,
)
val consumer = KafkaConsumer<String, String>(config)
consumer.subscribe(listOf("payments"))        // the group decides which partitions this member reads
```

try.title: Watch three consumers split six partitions
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the broker: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait`.

Run `GroupDemo` (command below). It writes 10 payments to each partition of the 6-partition topic `ledger-rebalance`, then starts three consumers of one new group, one after the other, on the new protocol. Each one prints what the group gives it and takes away. Before a partition leaves, its listener commits how far it got.
Predict before you run it: when c3 joins, which partitions does it get, and does c1 stop processing the ones it keeps?

Describe the group it used (the name is on the first line): `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --group <name>`.

try.expect:
On a fresh broker:
```text
mode consumer, group ledger-consumer-1794084212193
  0.0s  c1 joins
  6.9s  c1 assigned [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], starts at [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], owns [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
  7.1s  c2 joins
  8.0s  c1 revoked  [3, 4, 5], committed [10, 10, 10]
  8.8s  c2 assigned [3, 4, 5], starts at [10, 10, 10], owns [3, 4, 5]
  8.8s  c3 joins
  9.2s  c1 revoked  [2], committed [10]
  9.9s  c2 revoked  [5], committed [10]

```
Each new member took partitions only from the others' surplus, and c1 kept 0 and 1 the whole time. c3 got 2 and 5 one at a time, as c1 and c2 released them. Every new owner started at 10, the offset its predecessor committed. The first assignment takes longer on a fresh broker (here 6.9 s), because the broker creates `__consumer_offsets` on first use; your times will differ. try.title: Take the handover away
steps: Keep the broker running. Run `GroupDemo` again with `nohandover`: the listener no longer commits when a partition leaves, and nothing else commits either (command below).
Predict the last line: how many records will the group process, for how many records in the topic?

Trimmed:
```text
mode consumer, group ledger-consumer-1794084252054, no handover commits
  1.8s  c1 assigned [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], starts at [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], owns [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
  2.9s  c1 revoked  [3, 4, 5], committed nothing
  3.5s  c2 assigned [3, 4, 5], starts at [0, 0, 0], owns [3, 4, 5]
  4.2s  c1 revoked  [2], committed nothing
  4.7s  c2 revoked  [5], committed nothing
  4.8s  c3 assigned [2], starts at [0], owns [2]
  4.8s  c3 assigned [5], starts at [0], owns [2, 5]
records processed: 200, records in the topic: 120
```
The topic now holds 20 records per partition. c1 read all 120, but without a commit the group's bookmark for partitions 3, 4 and 5 stayed empty, so c2 started at offset 0 (`auto.offset.reset=earliest`) and read their 60 records again. c3 did the same for 2 and 5: 40 more. Five partitions moved and 80 payments were processed twice, by a perfectly ordinary scale-up.

sections.h: Eager, cooperative and the new protocol stop different things
sections.body:
How a group rebalances depends on the protocol it speaks, and Kafka 4.4 has two.

The **classic protocol** works in rounds. When membership changes, the coordinator tells every member to rejoin (a JoinGroup request), waits until all of them have, picks one member as the group leader, and lets that member run the assignor. Then it sends each member its share (SyncGroup). Two flavours run on top of it.

**Eager** is the original. A member rejoins empty-handed: before JoinGroup it revokes every partition it owns. Nothing is processed until the new assignment arrives, and a group with 100 members waits for the slowest of them. Frames 1 to 3 of the stepper show it. It is also what you get by default: the consumer's default `partition.assignment.strategy` is `[RangeAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor]`, and the docs say it uses Range, an eager assignor, until you remove Range from the list.

**Cooperative** rebalancing (KIP-429, Kafka 2.4) keeps the rounds but lets members keep their partitions while they rejoin. The assignor, `CooperativeStickyAssignor`, works out which partitions must move. Their owners revoke only those, and a second round assigns them. Nobody else stops, but every move costs two rounds.

The **new consumer group protocol** (KIP-848, generally available since Kafka 4.0) drops the rounds. Each member sends a heartbeat every few seconds and the coordinator answers. The coordinator runs the assignor itself (`uniform` by default, or `range`) whenever membership changes, and keeps a target assignment. Each member compares what it owns with its target and moves toward it on its own: first it revokes what it must give up, then the coordinator assigns it what others have released. There is no group-wide barrier, members that keep their partitions never notice, and there is no leader to wait for. Frames 4 to 6 show it.

You must opt in. The broker side is on by default in 4.0 and later, but the client default for `group.protocol` is still `classic` in 4.4. Set `group.protocol=consumer`. Three classic settings then belong to the broker instead: `session.timeout.ms`, `heartbeat.interval.ms` and `partition.assignment.strategy` all fail with a `ConfigException` if you set them on the client. The broker's `group.consumer.*` settings replace them, and `group.remote.assignor` picks a broker assignor. You can move a group from classic to the new protocol with a rolling restart, one instance at a time; the mixed group keeps working.

The new protocol has one cost: assignments travel on heartbeats, so a member learns about a change only on its next heartbeat, every 5 seconds by default (`group.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms`). The lab broker uses 1 second so the demos finish quickly.

refs.title: KIP-848: The next generation of the consumer rebalance protocol

sections.h: Two clocks decide when a member is gone
sections.body:
A rebalance also starts when the group decides a member is gone. It decides with two separate clocks, and they catch different failures.

The first clock checks that the process is alive. A background thread in the client sends heartbeats. If the coordinator hears nothing for the **session timeout**, 45 seconds by default, it removes the member and gives its partitions away. That catches a crash, a `kill -9` or a pulled network cable, and it means a crashed member's partitions sit unread for up to 45 seconds. A member that closes cleanly with `close()` leaves at once instead. On the classic protocol the client settings `session.timeout.ms` and `heartbeat.interval.ms` (3 s) control this clock; on the new one the broker's `group.consumer.session.timeout.ms` and `group.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms` do.

The second clock checks that your loop is making progress. Heartbeats keep flowing even while your code is stuck in a card-issuer call, so heartbeats alone can't catch that. If your code doesn't call `poll` again within `max.poll.interval.ms`, 5 minutes by default, the client leaves the group by itself. In `SlowConsumerDemo` c1 has a 4-second limit and one payment takes 8 seconds. At 4 seconds c1 leaves, and a second later c2 owns c1's partition and processes it from the last commit. When c1 comes back, it finishes the records it was holding, so they are processed twice. Its commit fails with `CommitFailedException`, and its next `poll` reports the partitions as lost and rejoins. Lesson 6 gave the fix: lower `max.poll.records` until a batch fits easily inside the limit.

Deploys are the third source of rebalances. A rolling restart of six instances means six leaves and six joins: twelve rebalances in a few minutes, with each partition moving to another member and back. **Static membership** stops that. Give each instance a stable `group.instance.id`, such as `ledger-3` for pod 3 of a StatefulSet. A static member that shuts down keeps its partitions, nobody else is disturbed, and when an instance with the same id comes back within the session timeout it gets the same partitions. The price is that if it doesn't come back, its partitions wait the full session timeout before anyone takes them.

How do you see a group falling behind? With **lag**, from lesson 1 of this track: for each partition, the log end offset minus the group's committed offset. `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe` prints it per partition. Lag that grows steadily means too few consumers or slow processing. Lag that jumps on every partition at once, again and again, usually means the group keeps rebalancing.

try.title: Stall a consumer, then restart one
steps: Run `SlowConsumerDemo` (command below). Two consumers share a new 2-partition topic. c1 has `max.poll.interval.ms=4000`, and pay-2 makes it wait 8 s for a card issuer that hangs.
Predict: who processes c1's partition while it waits, and what happens to c1's commit when it wakes up?

Then run `RestartDemo`, which stops c1 and starts it again 3 s later, like a deploy: first `./gradlew :kafka:demo -Pmain=sfz.kafka.l07.demo.RestartDemo`, then the same command with `-Pargs=static` (or `RestartDemoKt` for Kotlin). Watch c2's lines.
Stop the broker: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml down -v`.

try.expect:
`SlowConsumerDemo`:
```text
  3.0s  both members own one partition; writing pay-0 .. pay-9 to each
  3.0s  c1 assigned [1], starts at offset [0]
  3.6s  c1 partition 1: pay-2 calls the card issuer, which hangs for 8 s
  3.6s  c2 partition [0]: processed [pay-0, pay-1, pay-2, pay-3, pay-4]
  3.6s  c2 partition [0]: processed [pay-5, pay-6, pay-7, pay-8, pay-9]
  8.9s  c2 assigned [1], starts at offset [0]
  8.9s  c2 partition [1]: processed [pay-0, pay-1, pay-2, pay-3, pay-4]
  9.0s  c2 partition [1]: processed [pay-5, pay-6, pay-7, pay-8, pay-9]

```
About 4 s into the hang c1 left, and c2 took partition 1 from offset 0 and processed all ten. c1 then finished pay-0 to pay-4 as well: five payments processed twice. Its commit was refused, the listener heard `onPartitionsLost`, and c1 rejoined. Which consumer gets which partition first varies between runs. `RestartDemo` without `static` (trimmed):
```text
  5.1s  c1 shuts down for a deploy
  5.1s  c1 revoked  [1]
  6.0s  c2 assigned [1]
  8.2s  c1 starts again
  9.3s  c2 revoked  [1]
  9.7s  c1 assigned [1]
```
With `static`, c2 prints nothing at all between the shutdown and the restart:
```text
  6.4s  c1 shuts down for a deploy
  6.4s  c1 revoked  [0]
  9.6s  c1 starts again
 10.7s  c1 assigned [0]
```
A dynamic restart moved partition 1 twice. A static one moved nothing: the group kept c1's partition for it.

refs.title: Kafka 4.4 consumer configs: max.poll.interval.ms, group.instance.id, group.protocol

analogy: A consumer group is a team of cashiers and the partitions are checkout lanes. Each lane has one cashier at a time, so the customers in a lane are served in order, and each lane keeps its own tally sheet of how far it got. When a cashier arrives or goes home, the supervisor reassigns lanes. The old way (eager) is to close every lane, collect every tally sheet and hand out a new plan of who works which lane. The new way is to tap only the cashiers whose lanes move: they finish the customer in front of them, hand over the tally sheet, and the new cashier carries on from the last tick. The analogy breaks at the tally sheet: a real cashier can't forget to hand it over, but a Kafka consumer that commits nothing on revoke silently makes the next one serve the same customers again.
in_your_world: Your Quarkus payment services join groups through the SmallRye Kafka connector, so check what it passes to the client: on kafka-clients 4.x you can set `group.protocol=consumer` as an ordinary consumer property on the channel, and you then have to remove `session.timeout.ms` and `heartbeat.interval.ms`, which the client rejects with that protocol. Each pod of a Kubernetes StatefulSet has a stable name, which makes it a natural `group.instance.id`, so rolling deploys stop shuffling partitions. If a payment needs a slow call, such as a fraud check or an issuer that can take seconds, size `max.poll.records` so a full batch takes well under `max.poll.interval.ms`. If the work belongs in a Temporal workflow, start the workflow from the consumer and keep the poll loop fast. And alert on lag per partition, not just per group: one stuck partition hides inside a healthy average.
mistake: Leaving the defaults and assuming rebalances are cheap. The default classic assignor is eager, so every deploy, scale-up or slow batch stops the whole group, and teams see it only as lag spikes with no errors. It gets worse when processing is slow: a batch that overruns `max.poll.interval.ms` gets the member thrown out, which triggers a rebalance, which delays everyone's next poll, and the group rebalances in a loop. The fix: set `group.protocol=consumer` (or at least `CooperativeStickyAssignor`), commit in `onPartitionsRevoked`, keep batches well inside `max.poll.interval.ms` with a smaller `max.poll.records`, and use `group.instance.id` for instances that restart often.

compare.title: A rebalance listener that hands the bookmark over, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java

kotlin.title: Kotlin

compare.note: The same three callbacks. Java has to override `onPartitionsLost` to stop the interface's default, which simply calls `onPartitionsRevoked` and would commit a partition that is no longer yours; Kotlin's override does the same job. Kotlin builds the offsets map in one expression with `mapNotNull` and `toMap`, where Java fills a `HashMap` in a loop. Both keep `done` as a plain map, without locks: the consumer calls the listener on the polling thread, inside `poll`, so nothing else touches it at the same time.

steps.say: Subscribe with the handover listener, and tell it about every payment once it is applied. The loop still commits after each batch, so a crash replays at most one batch; the listener covers the moment a partition leaves between commits.

Roll it out one pod at a time. KIP-848 supports this online migration: during the roll the group holds members of both protocols, and the coordinator keeps it working. Watch it with `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group ledger --members`: each member has an id and its partitions, and lag stays flat while a pod restarts.

Check the three ways a member can leave. A clean shutdown (`close()`) revokes, commits, and for a static member keeps its partitions reserved until the session timeout. A crash replays from the last batch commit, which the idempotent ledger absorbs. A stuck batch past `max.poll.interval.ms` makes the member leave; its later commit fails with `CommitFailedException`, the listener gets `onPartitionsLost` and commits nothing. The lab's broker test grows a real group from one member to three and checks that no payment is processed twice.

lab.title: Build the assignors and a handover listener, then grow a real group
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All 16 fail. `AssignorsTest` and `StickyAssignorTest` need no broker; `HandoverListenerTest` drives your listener with `MockConsumer`, whose `rebalance` and `losePartitions` methods play the coordinator; `RebalanceOnBrokerTest` runs a real group on a Kafka 4.4 broker.
In `Assignors.java`, write `range` and `roundRobin`. Sort the members by id first, as Kafka does, and give every member an entry even when it gets nothing.

In `StickyAssignor.kt`, write `assign`: every member keeps what it owned, up to its quota (`partitions / members`, plus one for the first `partitions % members` members, with those extra slots going to the members that owned the most), then the leftover partitions are dealt to whoever still has room. Then write `toRevoke`.

In `HandoverListener.kt`, write the four functions: remember each processed record's next offset, commit the revoked partitions' offsets, record every event, and on `onPartitionsLost` forget without committing.

Run everything until all 16 pass. The broker test grows a group from one member to three, writing 60 records at each step, and checks that all 180 were processed exactly once: the poll loop never commits, so only your handover can make that true. It runs once with `group.protocol=consumer` and once with the classic eager protocol, and checks what each one revoked.
hints: Range per topic: with `n` partitions and `m` members, member `i` starts at `i * (n / m) + min(i, n % m)` and takes `n / m` partitions, plus one if `i < n % m`.
For the sticky quotas, sort members by how many of their old partitions still exist, largest first, then by id; the first `partitions % members` of that order get the extra slot.
In the listener, build the commit map only from partitions you have an offset for, and skip `commitSync` when it is empty.

drill.title: The handover listener from memory
drill.prompt: Write, from memory, a `ConsumerRebalanceListener` that commits the next offset to read of every revoked partition it has processed records for, and commits nothing for lost partitions. Then answer: under the new protocol, c4 joins a group in which c1 to c3 own two partitions each of a 6-partition topic. How many partitions does each old member revoke?

recap: A consumer group shares a topic by partition: each partition has exactly one owner in the group and one committed offset per group. Members beyond the partition count sit idle.
A rebalance moves partitions when members join or leave. Commit in `onPartitionsRevoked` so the next owner starts exactly where you stopped; never commit in `onPartitionsLost`.
The default classic assignor list uses Range, an eager assignor: every member hands back everything on every rebalance. Cooperative rebalancing moves only what must move, in two rounds.
The new protocol (KIP-848, `group.protocol=consumer`) lets the broker compute assignments and each member reconcile on its own: revoke first, then assign. The 4.4 client still defaults to classic.
Heartbeats and the session timeout (45 s) catch dead processes; `max.poll.interval.ms` (5 min) catches stuck loops. Static membership (`group.instance.id`) keeps partitions through a restart.

quiz.q: From lesson 6: c1 commits after each batch of 500. It has applied 300 records of a batch on partition 4 when a rebalance moves partition 4 to c2. c1 has no rebalance listener. What does c2 do?
options: It starts after the 300, because the group tracks c1's progress
It starts at the last committed offset, so up to 300 records are applied a second time
It waits until c1 finishes the batch, then starts after it
It starts at the log end, so the rest of c1's batch is skipped
quiz.why: The new owner can only start where the group's bookmark is, and c1 last committed before this batch. Kafka knows nothing about c1's in-memory progress, which is lesson 6's position versus committed offset. A commit in `onPartitionsRevoked` closes the gap; the idempotent ledger makes the replay harmless when the gap can't be closed, as after a crash.

quiz.q: A payments topic has 8 partitions. The ledger group runs 10 instances. What happens?
options: Each instance gets 0.8 of a partition's records
Kafka adds two partitions to the topic
Two partitions get two owners each
Two instances own no partitions and sit idle until another member leaves
quiz.why: In a consumer group a partition has exactly one owner, so parallelism stops at the partition count. The two extra members are spare capacity: they take over if a member dies. Kafka never adds partitions by itself, and two owners on one partition would break per-key order.

quiz.q: A group of three uses the classic protocol with `CooperativeStickyAssignor`. A fourth member joins. Which partitions stop being processed during the rebalance?
options: All of them, until the new assignment arrives
None at all
Only the partitions that move to the new member, while they move
Only the partitions of the group leader
quiz.why: Cooperative rebalancing lets members keep their partitions while they rejoin; only the owners of partitions that must move revoke them, and a second round hands them to the new member. The first option is eager rebalancing, which is what the default assignor list gives you.

quiz.q: A consumer's batches sometimes take 7 minutes because of a slow downstream API. Its heartbeats are fine. With default settings, what happens?
options: After 5 minutes without a `poll`, the client leaves the group; the partitions move, the batch is processed again by the new owner, and the old member's commit fails
Nothing: heartbeats prove it is alive
The session timeout expires and the coordinator removes it
The broker slows down its fetches
quiz.why: Heartbeats only prove the process is running; `max.poll.interval.ms` (300,000 ms) checks that the loop calls `poll`. Past it the client leaves on its own, which causes a rebalance and duplicate processing, and the late commit fails with `CommitFailedException`. The fix is a smaller `max.poll.records` or faster processing, not a longer session timeout.

quiz.q: The ledger runs six pods with static membership (`group.instance.id`) and the default 45-second session timeout. One pod's node fails and the pod never comes back. What happens to its partitions?
options: They move to the other members at once
They are unprocessed for about 45 seconds, then the coordinator gives them to other members
They stay unprocessed until the pod comes back
The whole group stops until an operator removes the member
quiz.why: A static member's partitions are kept for it until the session timeout passes, because it might be restarting. That is what makes a rolling deploy cheap, and it is the price here: the partitions wait out the full timeout, and lag builds on them. Then the coordinator removes the member and reassigns them as usual.

flashcards.front: How does a consumer group divide a topic?
flashcards.back: By partition: each partition has exactly one owner in the group at a time, and the group keeps one committed offset per partition.

flashcards.front: What does the default classic `partition.assignment.strategy` do on a rebalance?
flashcards.back: It is `[RangeAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor]` and uses Range, which is eager: every member hands back all its partitions first.

flashcards.front: How do you opt in to the KIP-848 protocol, and what must you remove?
flashcards.back: Set `group.protocol=consumer`. Remove `session.timeout.ms`, `heartbeat.interval.ms` and `partition.assignment.strategy`: the client rejects them.

flashcards.front: What should `onPartitionsRevoked` do, and what must `onPartitionsLost` not do?
flashcards.back: Revoked: commit the next offset to read of each partition you processed. Lost: don't commit, the partitions already belong to someone else.

flashcards.front: Which failure does `max.poll.interval.ms` catch that heartbeats can't?
flashcards.back: A loop that is stuck or too slow: heartbeats come from a background thread, so they keep flowing. Default 5 minutes.
The member is static: a restart within the session timeout gets the same partitions back without a rebalance.

terms.plain: Consumers with the same `group.id` that share a topic's partitions, one owner per partition, with one committed offset per partition.
The broker that manages a group's membership and stores its committed offsets.
The algorithm that maps partitions to members: range, round robin, sticky, or the broker's `uniform`.
Moving partitions between members because a member joined, left or was thrown out.
Every member hands back all its partitions before the new assignment, so the whole group stops.
Members keep their partitions during a rebalance and hand back only those that move.
Callbacks the consumer runs inside `poll` when partitions are assigned, revoked or lost.
A member with a fixed `group.instance.id`, whose partitions wait for it during a restart.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks why every deploy of the ledger service causes a lag spike on all partitions and a few duplicate payments in the logs. Explain what happens during the deploy and what you would change.
explain_back.answer: Each pod that stops leaves the group and each pod that starts joins it, so a rolling deploy causes one rebalance per step. We run the classic protocol with the default assignor, which is eager: on every rebalance every member hands back all of its partitions and waits for the new assignment, so all partitions stop at once. That is the lag spike. The duplicates come from the handover: our consumer commits after each batch but not in `onPartitionsRevoked`, so a partition that moves restarts at the last batch commit and the new owner reapplies what the old owner had already done; the idempotency check catches them, which is why we only see them in logs. I would switch to `group.protocol=consumer` so only the partitions that move pause, add a rebalance listener that commits processed offsets on revoke and commits nothing on lost, and give each pod a `group.instance.id` from its StatefulSet name, so a restarting pod keeps its partitions and nothing moves at all.

deeper.body:
**Epochs keep the new protocol honest.** KIP-848 tracks three counters. The group epoch goes up whenever membership or subscriptions change. The target assignment carries the epoch it was computed for. Each member has a member epoch, and it advances only once that member has reconciled to the target. A heartbeat or commit from a member with an old epoch is refused with `FENCED_MEMBER_EPOCH`, which is how the coordinator stops a member that missed a change from acting on stale partitions.

**Regex subscriptions moved to the broker.** With the new protocol, `subscribe(SubscriptionPattern)` sends an RE2/J pattern to the coordinator, which resolves it against the cluster's topics. A new topic that matches is picked up without every client polling metadata. Only the new protocol supports it.

**Range still matters for joins.** If two topics are partitioned the same way (say `payments` and `refunds`, both keyed by account and both with 12 partitions), Range gives partition 3 of both to the same member, so a consumer can join them locally. The broker's `range` assignor keeps that property; set `group.remote.assignor=range` to get it. The lab's test that one member gets the extra partition of every topic is that property seen from the other side.

**Share groups are a different tool.** Lesson 12 of this track covers share groups, where several members read the same partition and each record is acknowledged on its own. They give up per-partition order to get more consumers than partitions.
